title: Pipelining
summary: How a CPU overlaps instructions like an assembly line — one finishes almost every cycle, though none finishes any faster.

blocks.markdown:
**Pipelining** overlaps the stages of different instructions so several are in flight at once, instead of finishing one fully before starting the next.

- Like a **laundry assembly line**: wash, dry, fold, put away — while one load dries, the next is already washing.
- The CPU splits instruction execution into fixed **stages** and runs each stage on a different instruction, all in the same cycle.
- Goal: finish instructions faster **on average**, without making any single instruction faster.
- See [cpu-datapath](cpu-datapath) for the datapath this builds on.

Four loads of laundry, each needing wash, dry, fold — 30 minutes per step.

- **No overlap:** finish one load completely (90 min) before starting the next → 4 loads take 360 min.
- **Overlap:** start washing load 2 while load 1 dries. Loads finish every 30 min after the first one completes.
- Each **load** (laundry) is like an **instruction**; each **step** (wash/dry/fold) is like a pipeline **stage**.

blocks.subTitle: IF and ID
blocks.markdown:
A classic RISC pipeline splits every instruction into 5 fixed stages.

- **IF — Instruction Fetch:** read the next instruction from memory using the program counter.
- **ID — Instruction Decode:** figure out what the instruction means and read its source registers.

Every instruction passes through all 5 stages, one per cycle, in order.

blocks.subTitle: EX, MEM, WB
blocks.markdown:
The remaining three stages finish the work.

- **EX — Execute:** the ALU does the arithmetic or computes a memory address.
- **MEM — Memory Access:** read from or write to data memory (skipped by instructions that don't touch memory).
- **WB — Write Back:** the result is written back into a register.

Together: **IF → ID → EX → MEM → WB.**

Overlapping instructions, one stage each per clock cycle.

<<< Image: a pipeline timing diagram, rows = instructions 1-5, columns = clock cycles 1-9, each cell labelled with its stage abbreviation (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) forming a diagonal staircase pattern, blue/grey palette, clean grid lines, minimal text >>>

- Instruction 2 starts IF while instruction 1 is still in ID — every stage is busy, every cycle.
- By cycle 5, all five stages are active on five different instructions at once.

Pipelining trades one for the other — know which is which.

| Term | What it measures |
|---|---|
| Latency | Time for one instruction, start to finish |
| Throughput | Instructions completed per unit time |

Pipelining **improves throughput** (one instruction finishes almost every cycle) but does **not** shorten any single instruction's latency — it still takes 5 cycles start to finish.

A **pipeline register** sits between two stages and holds an instruction's data and results until the next clock edge, when it moves to the next stage.

- Registers **IF/ID**, **ID/EX**, **EX/MEM**, **MEM/WB** each latch one instruction's state.
- They let each stage work independently — a stage never has to wait on another mid-cycle.
- No pipeline registers means no pipelining: stages would blur into one long combinational block.

All stages share one clock, so every stage must fit in the same cycle time.

- The cycle time is set by the **slowest stage** — usually EX or MEM.
- A fast IF stage still waits for a slow EX stage; you can't run stages at different speeds.
- To speed up the whole pipeline, you must speed up (or split) its **slowest** stage.

For an **N-stage** pipeline, the best-case speedup over no pipelining approaches **N times**, once the pipeline is full of back-to-back instructions.

- A 5-stage pipeline could ideally run close to 5x faster in throughput.
- "Ideal" assumes every stage takes equal time and a new instruction enters every single cycle.
- Real pipelines fall short of this — that gap is the next thing to understand.

Two reasons real speedup lands below Nx.

- **Uneven stages:** if one stage is slower than the rest, the clock cycle is set by it, wasting time in every faster stage.
- **Hazards:** situations that stall or flush the pipeline, forcing bubbles (idle cycles) instead of steady one-per-cycle completion.
- Hazards are the bigger real-world cost — covered next in [pipeline-hazards](pipeline-hazards).

Common mistakes:

- **"Pipelining makes each instruction faster."** No — latency per instruction stays the same or grows slightly; only throughput improves.
- **"More stages always help."** More stages raise the ideal speedup but add more pipeline registers and more ways for hazards to bite.
- **"The pipeline is always full."** Hazards and stalls regularly leave stages idle.

blocks.subTitle: The 5 stages
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What are the 5 classic pipeline stages?**

**IF** (fetch instruction) → **ID** (decode, read registers) → **EX** (ALU computes) → **MEM** (access data memory) → **WB** (write result to a register). Each instruction moves through all five, one stage per clock cycle.

blocks.subTitle: Throughput or latency?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Does pipelining reduce latency or improve throughput?**

**Throughput.** A single instruction still takes 5 cycles end to end — sometimes slightly more due to pipeline overhead. What improves is how often an instruction *completes*: close to one per cycle once the pipeline is full, instead of one every 5 cycles.

blocks.subTitle: What limits clock speed
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What limits how fast you can clock a pipelined CPU?**

The **slowest stage**. Every stage shares one clock period, so the cycle time can't be shorter than the time the slowest stage needs. Speeding up the pipeline means speeding up, or splitting, that bottleneck stage.

blocks.subTitle: Ideal speedup formula
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the ideal speedup of an N-stage pipeline?**

Close to **N times** the throughput of a non-pipelined design, assuming equal-length stages and a steady stream of instructions filling the pipeline every cycle. It's a ceiling, not a guarantee.

blocks.subTitle: Why ideal speedup isn't hit
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why don't real pipelines hit the ideal N-times speedup?**

Stages are rarely equal length, so the clock is set by the slowest one. Worse, **hazards** — cases where the next instruction can't safely proceed this cycle (needing a result not ready yet, an unknown branch target, or clashing hardware) — force stalls or flushes that leave stages idle. See [pipeline-hazards](pipeline-hazards) for how each is handled.

blocks.subTitle: Role of pipeline registers
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What do pipeline registers actually do?**

They sit between adjacent stages and latch an instruction's data on each clock edge, so each stage can work on its own instruction independently. Without them, stages couldn't run concurrently — the logic would collapse into one long uncontrolled path.
